job: Oil pressure sensor or switch replacement
unit: One engine oil pressure sensor (also sold as an oil pressure switch or sending unit), fitted, with stored codes cleared. Not included: diagnosis of the oil light, gauge reading or code, a mechanical oil pressure test, an oil and filter change, intake manifold gaskets or seals on engines where the manifold comes off to reach the sensor, wiring or connector repair, and the separate valve-timing (rocker arm) oil pressure switch some engines also carry.

finding: The site has no live range for this job, so there is nothing to grade; these are first figures. Built totals (part + stated hours x $120-$160/hr, the national middle labor rate used for these checks), for one sensor: economy 2014 Dodge Dart 2.0L/2.4L about $88-$162 (0.5 hr); midsize 2014 Jeep Cherokee 3.2L V6 about $179-$247 (1.0 hr); truck 2014 Ram 1500 about $107-$407 (0.4 hr on the 5.7L V8 up to a seller's 2 hours; Chrysler's own time for the 3.6L V6 is 1.6 hr); large near-luxury 2014 Chrysler 300 about $143-$279 (0.7 hr on the 5.7L V8, 1.2 hr on the 3.6L V6). A supportable range is therefore roughly $90-$410, and where the sensor sits decides most of it. Against the benchmarks: RepairPal ($207-$261) falls in the middle of the built totals, and YourMechanic's vehicle pages ($182-$517) cover the same span and run higher at the top; its $517 for a 2013 Wrangler 3.6L is well above what Chrysler's 1.7 hr warranty time for that vehicle would build. Only two independent estimators were found (the two YourMechanic entries are one publisher), which is one short of the usual three. How solid the labor times are, stated plainly. All four classes rest on one Chrysler bulletin that names the example vehicles and prints the operation as 'Sensor, Oil Pressure - Replace' with times in hours: 0.5 on the Dart, 1.0 on the Cherokee 3.2L, 0.4 and 1.6 on the Ram 1500, 0.7 and 1.2 on the 300. Those are real maker times for the example vehicles, with diagnosis kept separate, but they are warranty times, the low end of what a shop bills, and for the economy and midsize classes no second stated time was found, so those labor ranges are a single point and a real quote will usually be somewhat higher. The truck high end is a parts seller's approximate 2-hour figure. Every example is a Chrysler-family vehicle because that was the only maker found printing a clean replacement time with a unit. The luxury class is the weakest fit: the example is a near-luxury sedan, not a luxury-brand car. Acura's bulletin for the MDX, RL, TL, TSX V6 and ZDX prints 0.3 and 0.4 for the engine oil pressure switch, but with no unit and read from a forum copy, so it is a cross-check only; if it is hours, a luxury-brand V6 with an easy-to-reach switch would build lower than the 300. Sensor location: the same Mopar sensor takes 0.4 hr on the Ram 5.7L V8 and 1.6 hr on the Ram 3.6L V6, where the bulletin lists intake plenum and intake manifold seals; Kia allows 1.6-1.8 man-hours on its 3.3L V6, where intake gaskets are replaced with the switch. Chevrolet Silverado, GMC Sierra and Tahoe 5.3L V8: on the 2007-2013 generation the sensor sits at the back of the engine behind the intake manifold, close to the firewall, and some shops remove the intake to reach it, so it costs more labor than an easy-access sensor. That statement rests on weak sources (an owners' forum thread on a 2008 Tahoe 5.3L and a parts seller's guide); no General Motors page stating the Silverado location was loaded, and no maker time for it was found. The GM bulletins loaded name an 'Engine Oil Pressure Sensor Replacement' operation but print 'use published time' instead of a figure; one of them (PIP5932D, 1.2L Encore GX, Envista, Trailblazer and Trax) says the sensor is reached by removing the intake manifold. Expect a Silverado quote toward the upper part of the truck range or above it. Parts: genuine list prices are from dealer catalog pages ($81.70 for the Dart sensor, $86.70 for the sensor shared by the Cherokee V6, Ram 1500 and 300). Only the Dart low end is a new aftermarket part ($28.27, on a page that lists the Dart without model years). For the other three classes the aftermarket prices found ($28.58, $34.19 and $44.99) were on pages that did not say new, so the low end is the genuine sensor at a dealer's discounted online price ($58.50); the Ram and Cherokee catalog pages are for the 2015 and 2016 model years with the same part number the bulletin names. An estimate is not a quote and not a diagnosis.
extras: A quote often adds a diagnosis fee, and many shops confirm real oil pressure with a mechanical gauge before replacing the sensor, billed separately. Where the intake manifold comes off to reach the sensor (the Chrysler 3.6L and 3.2L V6, some General Motors V8 trucks, the Kia 3.3L V6), new intake manifold gaskets or seals are added. Also common: an oil and filter change or an oil top-up, a new connector or wiring repair when the plug is oil-soaked, a sensor screen or filter on engines that have one, shop supplies and sales tax. Some engines carry a second, separate oil pressure switch for the valve timing system, quoted on its own.
held_reason: Held at review after one attempt: every class is a Chrysler-family vehicle on one bulletin, the luxury example (Chrysler 300) is not a luxury make, and benchmarks are short of three publishers. Needs a luxury-make example with a maker time printed with a unit.
